extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, students of aesthetics, and serious readers of poetic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for evaluating and producing poetry (especially distinctions between 'simple' or pastoral poetry and 'sentimental' or idealizing poetry), including criteria on choice of object, form vs. ideality, language, balance of faculties, and aims of poetic recreation vs. moral ennobling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal value: form vs. matter (individuality vs. ideality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every kind of poetry is bound to possess an infinite ideal value which it can satisfy in two different ways: (1) by giving the feeling of the infinite as to form, 'by representing the object altogether limited and individualizing it' (simple poetry), or (2) by awakening the feeling of the infinite as to matter, 'in freeing its object from all limits... by idealizing this object' (sentimental poetry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which mode (form/individuality or matter/ideality) you are pursuing and pursue it consistently. The text repeatedly advises against trying to combine both modes incompletely; doing so produces equivocal works that satisfy neither aesthetic demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commit to individuality or ideality (do not mix half-way)
rubrics_metrics.description: We must once for all declare either for individuality or ideality; to aspire to give satisfaction to both exigencies is, unless at perfection, 'to miss both ends.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If imitating 'simple' (Greek) poetry, do so exclusively and accept the limits of that form; if pursuing the sentimental/ideal, pursue it fully without conciliating merely sensuous requirements. Mixed aims produce equivocal effects in both subject-matter and language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity to nature for simple poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The simple poet is not exposed to failure in value so long as he keeps faithfully to nature, which is always completely circumscribed, that is, is infinite as regards form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For simple/pastoral poetry, prioritize detailed, definite representation of sensuous reality and individual truth. Rely on 'true nature' (not mere actuality) and aim for the sensuous, particular depiction that yields the feeling of the infinite as form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of object for sentimental poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The sentimental poet, wishing to give an absolute value to a particular object, should not borrow the simple poet's narrow pastoral objects; he ought to 'depart from the simple poet, just in the choice of object' because only by the nature of the objects can he resume the upper hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select objects or frames that allow idealization; avoid trying to graft lofty ideals onto inherently narrow or merely pastoral matter, which will neither charm by nature nor satisfy as pure ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of language and form (avoid floating between poetry and prose)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet who seeks to unite the simple with the sentimental often produces language 'which floats undecided between poetry and prose, as if he feared either to depart too far from nature, by speaking rhythmical language, or if he completely freed himself from rhythm, to lose all poetic flight.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align diction and rhetorical form with the chosen poetic aim. Avoid an undecided tone that undermines both poetic flight and fidelity to nature; choose whether rhythmic/poetic diction or freer prose-style better serves your objective and commit to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idyl ideal: reconcile real and ideal; calm of accomplishment with movement
rubrics_metrics.description: An idyl conceived rightly should realize 'the idea of humanity definitely reconciled with itself,' reconciling contradictions between the real and the ideal; the dominant expression should be calm 'that follows the accomplishment, and not that of indolence' while still expressing movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for unity that does not suppress variety: create calm born of equilibrium and fullness of strength rather than inert repose. Ensure movement is present (necessary for affecting readers) even in a reconciled, calm poetic atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent humanity in its highest moral value (unity and sensuous reality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple poetry has the favor to 'represent, in the real world, humanity at its highest value' by setting forth as a real fact what sentimental poetry only aspires to reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the goal is to evoke human fullness through realistic depiction, ensure the subject-matter and presentation convey dignity and the fulness of physical and spiritual life—unity of faculties—so readers feel both activity and sensuous completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confusion between actual nature and true nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual nature exists everywhere, but 'true nature' is rare because it requires an internal necessity. Criticism and practice err when they applaud mere actuality as if it were true human nature, leading to trivialities being tolerated as 'real nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake mere actuality, vulgarity, or caricature for poetic truth. True poetic depiction requires an inward necessity and dignity; check whether the portrayed behavior expresses genuine human nature or simply commonplace, base phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against vulgarity, platitude, and trivial imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple poetry's ease of expression invites vulgar imitators, producing 'incredible trivialities' and pleasantries that are 'pitiful.' Works that merely mimic everyday character without poetic capacity result in platitude, insipidity, or baseness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect poetic work from banal, comic caricature or trivial sentimental songs. Ensure that even comic or satirical portrayals are handled by a poet capable of raising the object; avoid easy, crowd-pleasing mimicry that substitutes for true inspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal necessity and preparedness of the poet (inspiration free of temporal need)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet ought to banish 'every trace of a temporal need' at the moment of inspiration; the simple genius must have an 'absolute freedom' and be prepared by anterior exercise to 'embrace all things with all his humanity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate readiness through practice and broad experience so inspiration rests on internal necessity, not on contingent wants or momentary constraints. The artist's mastery requires prior discipline to avoid dependence on accidental impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance receptivity and activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple genius tends to receptivity over activity; sentimental genius tends to activity over receptivity. The text warns both extremes are dangerous: 'inspiration without an object, and object without inspiration, are both negations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for a proportion between receptive responsiveness to the world and active imaginative formation. Assess whether the work is merely felt (no shaping) or merely conceived (no living sensuous anchor) and correct the imbalance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overstraining/exaggeration beyond possible human experience
rubrics_metrics.description: When thought is carried so far that 'no experience corresponds to it' or it is 'repugnant to the conditions of all possible experience,' the result is not poetic but an exaggerated, non-representable conception that nullifies poetic truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep idealization within the bounds of human possibility and sensuous truth. If portraying superhuman or absolute objects, either acknowledge their non-representability or humanize them so imagination has sensible limits; otherwise you risk nonsense or extravagant fantasy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate extravagance of feeling from extravagance of portraiture
rubrics_metrics.description: Extravagance of feeling can be 'true' and 'come from the heart' even if its object is artificial; but 'extravagance of portraiture' signals a cold heart and lack of poetic capacity and is mainly the fault of imitators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow intense, exaggerated feeling when it arises organically and retains simplicity of expression; avoid exaggerated, artificial depiction of characters or scenes that reveal imitation without internal life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's proper aim: harmonize sensuous recreation and moral ennobling
rubrics_metrics.description: Two maxims (poetry as amusement/recreation and poetry as moral ennobling) are correct but dangerous if taken to extremes. The poet's aim should free human nature from accidental hindrances without destroying essential human limits—'the aim is to harmonize spirit and sense.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject purely sensuous entertainment that suspends thought and reject a purely didactic or infinite moral ideal that demands impossible perfection. Seek a balanced aim that addresses all faculties and produces genuine aesthetic harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider reader's state: require full faculties for true aesthetic judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty 'addresses all the faculties of man' and can only be appreciated if a reader 'employs fully all his strength.' Many readers are too exhausted or narrowly occupied to judge true beauty, favoring mere recreation instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or evaluating serious poetic work, be aware of the intended audience's capacity for engagement. Do not conflate popular success among fatigued readers with genuine aesthetic achievement; design works appropriate to the expected readerly engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware that masterpieces may spawn cheap imitators
rubrics_metrics.description: Masterpieces of simple poetry are commonly 'followed by a host of stale and unprofitable works,' and masterpieces of the sentimental class by 'wild and fanciful effusions' from incompetent imitators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when a theme or form is likely to invite superficial imitation; guard originality by depth of handling and internal necessity so that derivative attempts are exposed as trivial rather than mistaken for the original's value.
